comments.author: btilly
comments.story_title: Why good managers are so rare
comments.why_zh: 自主权、精通、目的；关于动机说得非常准确。
comments.quote_zh: 想明白这为什么重要，去看
comments.text_zh: 上一任经理非常擅长“以激励来领导”。他让人自我感觉良好，觉得自己在学到东西，觉得自己既为自己那一小块天地、也为整个组织带来了改变。新经理则擅长跟踪事务和微观管理。但她能想出的最鼓舞人心的一句话却是：“你还有工作。”（我真希望自己是在开玩笑。）她还有个不幸的习惯：经常撒谎，而且撒得很拙劣，结果就是信任被摧毁。不过这方面我现在太愤懑了，不想讨论。想明白这为什么重要，去看 [VIDEO]。我认为它的信息并不完整（比如我注意到，压力与脑力表现之间的相关性高度取决于你正在做的脑力任务），但它关于动机的说法非常准确。关键因素是自主权（Autonomy）、精通（Mastery）和目的（Purpose）。好的领导者能让人同时感受到这三者，同时还能让他们去做组织需要他们做的事。微观管理把组织想要什么说得很清楚，却摧毁了动机。
comments.text: The previous manager was very good at "leading through inspiration". He made people feel good about themselves, feel like they were learning, and feel like they were making a difference both for their corner of the world and the whole organization. The new manager was good at keeping track of things and micromanaging. But the most inspiring line she could come up with was, "You still have a job." (I wish I was kidding.) She also had an unfortunate habit of lying badly and often, with a resulting destruction of trust. But that aspect I'm too bitter about at the moment to want to discuss. To see why it matters, go watch [VIDEO] . I believe that its message is not complete (for instance I've noticed that correlations between stress and mental performance is highly dependent upon the mental task you are doing), but what it says about motivation is spot on. The key factors are Autonomy, Mastery and Purpose. Good leaders can give people the sense of all three while still getting them to do what the organization needs them to do. Micromanagement makes it clear what the organization wants, but destroys motivation.

comments.author: sgentle
comments.story_title: Ask HN: No intrinisic motivation to build stuff
comments.why_zh: 对 Pink《Drive》的简短而出色的总结。
comments.quote_zh: 这里实际上总结得非常好
comments.text_zh: Steven Covey 的《The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People》是一本相当有开创性的个人管理书。就“基础性”材料而言，这是我的首推。它没多少实用工具，但里面的理念到处都用得上。如果你有兴趣进一步了解创造性动机，我会推荐 Dan Pink 的《Drive》。这本书挺短，而且这里有一份非常好的总结：[VIDEO] Tom DeMarco 和 Timothy Lister 的《Peopleware》是非常好的、针对程序员的管理材料。他们引用了大量对不同工作场所生产力做基准测试的研究，所以非常“X 好，X 坏”。Jim Collins 的《Good to Great》考察成功与失败的企业，以及让它们走到那一步的特质，本质上是他和团队对一批在 10 年间大幅跑赢股市的企业所做纵向研究的扩展总结。它更偏领导力而不是管理，但仍然非常有用。还有一本我还没读（都怪我那愚蠢地长的阅读清单），但仅凭名声就推荐的是 Marcus Buckingham 和 Curt Coffman 的《First, Break All The Rules》。这里有个总结：[LINK] 我跟你一样对那种废话连篇的博客文章感到沮丧。除了《First, Break All The Rules》（还没读）和《7 Habits》（我原谅它，因为它实在太好了）之外，我提到的书都基于书中引用的真实研究，而不只是某个家伙在说“我这么想是因为我懂很多东西”。
comments.text: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People by Steven Covey is a pretty seminal personal management book. It's my top recommendation in terms of "foundational" material. It's not got much in the way of practical tools, but the ideas are applicable everywhere. I would recommend Drive by Dan Pink if you're interested in learning more about creative motivation. It's pretty short, and actually very well summarised here: [VIDEO] Peopleware by Tom DeMarco and Timothy Lister is very good programmer-specific management material. They cite a lot of work benchmarking the productivity of different workplaces, so it's very "x is good, x is bad". Jim Collins' Good to Great is an examination of businesses that succeed vs fail, and the attributes that get them there, it's essentially an extended summary of a longitudinal study he and his team did of businesses that outperformed the stock market by a high factor over 10 years. It's more leadership than management, but still very useful. One that I haven't read yet (damn my stupidly big reading list) but recommend on reputation alone is First, Break All The Rules by Marcus Buckingham and Curt Coffman. Here's a summary: [LINK] I share your frustration about blah-blah blog posts. With the exception of First, Break All The Rules (which I haven't read yet) and 7 Habits (which I forgive because it's so damn good), the books I mention are based on actual research which is cited in the book, not just some dude going "I think this because I know stuff".

comments.author: Pkeod
comments.story_title: Netflix's Culture Document (2009)
comments.text_zh: [VIDEO] 足够高的薪水加上优厚的福利，高到需求得到满足，才是理想状态。“Rockstar”也许能和那些想招这类人的公司谈判，但如果你只招最优秀的人，而不是最适合你公司的人，那你的文化就会受损。我喜欢 Valve 的做法。没有 WallSt 或 Hollywood 那种 rockstar 文化。每个人都获得平等对待和认可。如果同事们认为你应得，你就能赚得更多——那里的人不是在追逐奖励——他们在做好自己热爱的事，并因此得到回报。这似乎对他们以及其他类似合作社式的公司非常有效。
comments.text: [VIDEO] High enough salary + great benefits to the point where needs are met are ideal. "Rockstars" may be able to negotiate with companies who want to hire those kinds of people, but if you are hiring only the best people and not the best people for your company then your culture will suffer. I like the way Valve does things. No rockstar culture like WallSt or Hollywood has. Everyone gets even footing and credit. You can earn more if your peers agree that you deserve it - people there are not chasing rewards - they are doing what they love well and being rewarded for it. It seems to work very well for them and other co-op like companies.

comments.author: Ygg2
comments.story_title: The Highest-Paid CEOs Are The Worst Performers, New Study Says
comments.why_zh: 支持自主权、精通和目的优于金钱。
comments.quote_zh: 如果你给人们更多自主权、精通和目的，他们就会表现得更好。
comments.text_zh: 我认为不是。那些薪酬最高、从事非重复性体力劳动的人，绩效评分却最差，一次又一次都是如此。所以，除非 CEO 的薪酬是付给他们手工拧螺栓或把球投进篮筐的，否则他们大概做得并不好，部分原因就在于有人给他们钱。金钱会引入恐惧（比如害怕赚不到足够的钱，或者害怕失去自己那份高薪职位），而这会导致视野狭窄。如果你给人们更多自主权、精通和目的，他们就会表现得更好。[VIDEO]
comments.text: I'd argue it's not. People that are paid most to do a job that isn't repetitive manual labor have worst performance scores, time and time again. So unless CEOs are paid to manually bolt things or throws ball into a hoop, they probably aren't doing well because, in part, they are given money. Money introduces fear (i.e. fear that you won't make enough money or lose your position with lots of money) and that leads to tunnel vision. People give more performance if you give them more autonomy, mastery and purpose. [VIDEO]

comments.why_zh: 被引用来讨论薪酬变化是否影响动机。
comments.text_zh: 通常，电影明星会在合同里谈下总收入的一小部分百分比。他们过去谈的是利润分成，但制片厂变得非常擅长摆弄影片的账目，直到一部成功的电影也几乎没有利润。我不明白为什么不能对软件工程师这么做。不过那本质上就是分红，而成长型公司为什么不想这么做也很明显。但同样不清楚的是，股票期权是否产生了预期的激励效果（甚至也不清楚加薪或某种利润分享是否会产生预期效果[1]）。我认为很明显，股票期权对于预期目的是次优的，但我不清楚该怎么解决。[1] [VIDEO]
comments.text: Typically movie stars negotiate a tiny % of gross revenue in their contract. They used to negotiate for % of profit, but studios got very good at fiddling with the numbers for the film until a successful movie had nearly no profit. I don't see why that can't be done for software engineers. That is essentially dividends though, and it's obvious why growth companies don't want to do that. But it's also not clear that stock options have the intended motivating effect (it's not even clear that increases in salary or some kind of profit sharing would have the intended effect either[1]) I think it's clear that stock options are sub-optimal for the intended purpose, but it's not obvious to me how to fix that. [1] [VIDEO]
